sentences: The most famous name in electric cars belongs to a man who died broke.
January 7th, 1943.
New York City.
In room 3327 of the Hotel New Yorker, an 86-year-old inventor dies alone, deep in debt.
Sixty years later, a startup in California puts his name on a car company.
Today, it's one of the most valuable car companies on Earth.
And the strangest part?
For years, the company named after him didn't even own its own name online.
We'll get to that.
This is the story of Nikola Tesla.
The man, the myths, and the brand.
Nikola Tesla was born in 1856, in a small village in what is now Croatia, to a Serbian family.
His father was a priest.
His mother, he said, invented gadgets for the household.
He studied engineering, worked for telephone and electric companies in Europe, and in 1884, he sailed to New York, with almost nothing in his pockets.
He had a remarkable memory.
He claimed he could picture entire machines in his head, and test them there, before building anything.
He landed a job working for Thomas Edison.
And this is where the first famous story comes in.
According to Tesla, Edison promised him $50,000 to improve his generators.
When Tesla delivered, Edison supposedly laughed, and told him he didn't understand American humor.
That story comes from Tesla himself, and some historians doubt the details.
But either way, he quit within the year.
His first company of his own pushed him out.
By his own account, he ended up digging ditches for a living.
But Tesla had an idea he'd carried since his student days: a motor that ran on alternating current, with no brushes and no sparking contacts, almost nothing to wear out.
The trick was something called a rotating magnetic field.
Feed alternating currents into coils around a ring, slightly out of step with each other, and the magnetic field itself spins.
Put a metal rotor in the middle, and the field drags it around.
In 1888, he patented his AC induction motor, and presented it to the country's top electrical engineers.
One man was paying very close attention: George Westinghouse.
He licensed Tesla's patents, and hired him.
Remember this motor.
It's coming back, more than a century later.
There was just one problem.
Edison had bet everything on direct current, and he wasn't giving up without a fight.
It became known as the War of the Currents.
Edison's camp warned that alternating current was deadly, and pointed to its use in the first electric chair.
An engineer allied with Edison's side even electrocuted animals in public demonstrations, to show how dangerous AC could be.
Tesla fought back with showmanship.
In his lectures, he let high-frequency current pass through his own body, lighting up lamps in his hands.
But AC had a huge advantage.
It could be sent long distances efficiently.
Direct current, back then, couldn't.
In 1893, Westinghouse lit up the Chicago World's Fair.
Millions of visitors saw a glowing white city running on alternating current.
Then came Niagara Falls.
In 1896, power generated at the falls, using Tesla's system, reached the city of Buffalo, more than 20 miles away.
Alternating current won.
It's the kind of power coming out of your wall right now.
So Tesla should have been rich, right?
Here's where it goes wrong.
Westinghouse's company ran into serious money trouble.
Tesla agreed to give up his royalties, and in 1897, he took a lump sum of about $216,000 for his patents.
That was a lot of money in 1897.
But it was a tiny slice of what those royalties could have become.
And in 1895, a fire tore through his New York laboratory, destroying years of equipment and notes.
Then Tesla went all in on his biggest dream: wireless power.
On Long Island, he built a giant tower called Wardenclyffe, funded with $150,000 from the banker J.
P.
Morgan.
The plan was to send messages, and eventually power, through the air and the earth itself.
But the money ran out, and Morgan wouldn't invest more.
The tower never did what he hoped.
Tesla lost the property to his creditors, and in 1917, the tower was demolished for scrap.
For the rest of his life, Tesla moved from hotel to hotel, often behind on the bills, feeding pigeons, and announcing inventions that never appeared.
He even told his biographer that he loved one white pigeon, the way a man loves a woman.
And that's where the myths start piling up.
Let's sort out a few.
Myth number one: Tesla tore up a contract worth billions, to save his friend Westinghouse.
What we can document is the buyout: a lump sum instead of royalties.
The dramatic tearing moment is much harder to prove.
Myth number two: he built a death ray.
In the 1930s, he told reporters he'd designed a beam that could stop armies from far away.
There's no evidence he ever built one.
Myth number three: the Supreme Court declared Tesla the inventor of radio.
In 1943, the court did knock out key parts of Marconi's radio patent, citing earlier work by Tesla and others.
But it never named Tesla the inventor of radio.
And the big one: Tesla invented everything.
He didn't.
But he did help build the electric world we live in.
There's even a scientific unit of magnetism called the tesla.
He died in 1943, in that hotel room.
Afterward, the government took his belongings and papers.
Now fast forward sixty years.
July 1st, 2003.
Two engineers in California, Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning, start an electric car company.
Eberhard is credited with choosing the name: Tesla Motors.
A tribute to the inventor.
But also a perfect fit, because their first car, the Roadster, would run on an AC induction motor.
The same kind of motor Tesla patented in 1888.
Elon Musk joined in 2004.
He led the first big funding round, with $6.5 million of his own money, and became chairman.
Later, he became the CEO.
The Roadster finally hit the road in 2008.
Only about 2,500 were ever built.
It was built on a modified Lotus sports car chassis, packed with thousands of small, laptop-style battery cells.
And then it got messy.
Eberhard sued.
The settlement, in 2009, allowed five people to call themselves co-founders, Musk included.
Here's the part that sounds made up.
For years, the company didn't even own tesla.com.
That address had belonged to a man named Stu Grossman since 1992.
Tesla finally got it in 2016.
Musk later said it cost $11 million, and took more than a decade.
In 2017, the company dropped "Motors" from its name.
Today, it's simply Tesla.
So here's the full circle.
A man who died broke, in debt, alone in a hotel room.
And more than a century after he patented his motor, his name became one of the most famous brands in the world.
No way.
